analysis.one_liner: Gives shareholders a bigger say over corporate boards and executive pay.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 12, 2009 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee the same day, the Shareholder Empowerment Act never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced public companies to open their official shareholder ballots to rivals: investors who held 1% of a company's stock for two years could nominate their own director candidates, directors would have had to win a majority of votes to keep their seats in uncontested elections, and brokers could no longer vote customer shares when the owner gave no instructions. On pay, shareholders would have gotten an annual nonbinding vote on executive compensation, boards would have needed clawback policies for bonuses later shown unearned, executives fired for poor performance would have lost their severance, and companies would have had to disclose the targets used to award bonuses and stock incentives.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders of public companies, above all long-term institutional holders — pension funds and mutual funds that manage ordinary workers' retirement savings — would gain a real path onto the company's own ballot for board nominees, majority-vote accountability for directors, an annual vote on executive pay, and clearer disclosure of how bonuses are earned. Executives would face clawbacks of unearned pay and the loss of severance for poor performance.

how_it_helps.text: Investors holding 1% of a company's voting shares for at least two years could nominate director candidates that appear on the company's own ballot, up to fewer than a majority of the board.
Directors would need a majority of votes cast to win uncontested elections, and a director who loses would have to offer to resign.
Brokers could no longer vote shares in uncontested director elections without specific instructions from the shares' actual owners, ending a practice that reliably favored management's picks.
Shareholders would get an annual, nonbinding vote on senior executive pay, and companies would have to disclose the performance targets used to award bonuses and stock incentives.

Boards would need clawback policies to recover bonuses later shown unearned — for example after fraud or restated financial statements — and could not pay severance to senior executives terminated for poor performance.
Advisers hired to negotiate executive pay would have to be independent of the company and its executives, and companies could not indemnify or shield them from liability.
Boards would be pushed, to the extent possible, to have an independent chair who has not served as a company executive.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate executives and boards would lose discretion over elections and pay; listed companies would bear new compliance and disclosure costs; brokers would lose the right to vote uninstructed customer shares; compensation consultants would lose conflicted engagements and liability shields.

drawbacks.text: The annual shareholder vote on executive pay is explicitly nonbinding — the bill states it cannot overrule the board's decisions or create any new fiduciary duty, so boards could ignore it.

Majority voting and the resignation policy apply only 'to the extent permitted under State law,' and the independent-chair requirement applies only 'to the extent possible,' so state corporate law and existing executive contracts could blunt the mandates.

Proxy access is limited to holders of 1% of voting securities held for at least two years, so the new leverage would flow mainly to large institutions; small investors rarely meet that threshold on their own.

The clawback policy requires recovery of unearned pay only 'to the extent that it is feasible and practical,' and the board itself decides when an executive's firing counts as poor performance — wide self-policing discretion.
The listing rules would apply to every listed company, not just badly governed ones, adding compliance and disclosure costs and litigation exposure across thousands of firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest parts of this bill were real: letting 1% long-term holders put rival nominees on the company's own ballot, requiring directors to win majorities to keep seats, and stopping brokers from voting uninstructed shares would have shifted actual power from management to the people who own the companies, at the cost mainly of compliance work for listed firms and lost protections for executives. The weaker parts undercut it: the annual pay vote is explicitly nonbinding, boards define when a firing counts as poor performance, clawbacks apply only where recovery is feasible, and key rules defer to state corporate law, so much of the bill would have been symbolic. The 1% two-year access threshold also means the new leverage would flow mostly to large institutions rather than small investors. On balance a genuine but moderate governance reform — and because it died in committee, none of it was ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gary Peters (D-MI) introduced the bill on June 12, 2009, joined at introduction by Reps. Waters, Dingell, Welch, Holt, DeFazio, and Capuano.
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day.
Eleven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The committee recorded no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill for the rest of the Congress, and it died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and boards of public companies kept the status quo — no shareholder access to the proxy ballot, no majority-vote requirement, no annual pay vote, and no clawback or severance restrictions — because the bill died in committee without a vote.

for.name: Rep. Gary C. Peters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Shareholder Empowerment Act of 2009 and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 12, 2009 and recorded no hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill died without action in the Democratic-led Financial Services Committee with no Republican support.

industries.industry: Corporate executives and boards of directors of public companies
industries.note: The bill would have let 1% long-term holders nominate rival directors on the company's own ballot, made directors win majority votes to keep seats, required an annual pay vote, clawbacks of unearned bonuses, and barred severance for executives fired for poor performance. Because the bill died, management kept its current control over board elections and pay.

industries.industry: Compensation consultants and pay advisory firms
industries.note: Advisers negotiating executive pay would have had to be independent of the company and its executives, could not hold equity or be paid through other engagements in ways that create conflicts, and could not be indemnified by the company. Firms that combined pay advice with other services would have lost that business.

Brokers would lose the ability to vote customer shares in uncontested director elections when the owner gave no instructions — votes that routinely went to management's slate. The benefit flows to shareholders who want their own votes to count.

industries.industry: Institutional investors — pension funds and mutual funds
industries.note: Proxy access, majority voting, and say on pay give large long-term holders — the funds that manage ordinary workers' retirement savings — real leverage over boards and executive compensation. Their interest in this bill runs alongside that of the savers they represent.
